Consul includes a distributed KV store often used for feature flags, dynamic configuration, and service configuration. Not typically used in service mesh scenarios but frequently used alongside it in HashiCorp-heavy stacks (Vault + Consul + Nomad).
Best multi-datacenter story. Works outside Kubernetes (VMs, ECS, Nomad). Simpler operational model for heterogeneous infrastructure. Integrated service catalog and health checking before adding mesh.

Multi-DC or hybrid cloud deployments. Organizations that also run workloads on VMs or ECS. Teams already using HashiCorp stack (Vault, Nomad, Terraform). When service discovery and health checking are needed independent of mesh.

Lighter L7 traffic management than Istio in open-source. Intentions model is simpler but less expressive than Istio AuthorizationPolicy. No ambient-mode equivalent. Enterprise features (advanced federation, audit logging, OIDC namespace isolation) require paid license.
Some important features (namespace isolation, audit logging, OIDC provider, read replicas, network segments) are in Consul Enterprise or HCP Consul, not OSS. Be aware when evaluating total cost.
Practical equivalents across Istio and Consul. Not perfect matches — the operational models differ significantly.

Both handle node/pod-level L4 interception with mTLS and identity. ztunnel is a shared node-level DaemonSet (lower overhead). Consul transparent proxy is per-sidecar in a pod. Consul has no node-level shared L4 proxy equivalent.
Waypoints ↔ Consul API Gateway / Terminating GW
Waypoints are shared L7 policy enforcement points deployed per namespace or service. Consul's nearest fit is API Gateway (ingress L7) or dedicated proxy-based enforcement at boundaries.

Istio VirtualService maps to Consul's ServiceRouter (L7 routing rules) and ServiceSplitter (traffic splitting) config entries. Istio's API is more expressive for complex routing; Consul's is simpler to get started.
Istio DestinationRule (subsets, load balancing, circuit breaker) maps to Consul ServiceResolver (failover, redirect, load balancer config) and ServiceDefaults (connection limits).

Both enforce allow/deny between services. Istio AuthorizationPolicy is richer: JWT claims, HTTP method/path, namespace, source principal. Consul Intentions are simpler: service-to-service allow/deny, plus L7 intentions for HTTP method/path matching in enterprise.

Both issue short-lived x509 SVIDs to workloads for mTLS identity. Istio Citadel uses Kubernetes ServiceAccount JWTs as proof-of-identity. Consul CA uses Consul auth methods (K8s service account, Vault) to issue certificates. Both support plugging in an external CA (Vault).

For mesh-to-external-service traffic: Istio uses ServiceEntry to register the external service and optionally routes through an Egress Gateway. Consul uses a Terminating Gateway to proxy outbound connections to services outside the mesh.
Ambient Mesh (no sidecar) ↔ No Consul equivalent

Istio ambient mesh removes most sidecars via ztunnel + waypoints. Consul still requires per-workload Envoy sidecars in its service mesh model. This is a meaningful architectural gap when resource efficiency is a priority.
Use this branch to reason about which mesh (or no mesh) is right for a given context.

You are Kubernetes-only or primarily Kubernetes. You need deep L7 traffic management (VirtualService, fault injection, progressive delivery with Argo Rollouts/Flagger). You want the richest CNCF-graduated open-source mesh. You care about ambient mode for resource efficiency at scale.

You have a hybrid environment (Kubernetes + VMs, ECS, Nomad, bare metal). You need multi-datacenter service mesh with WAN federation. You are already using the HashiCorp stack (Vault for secrets, Nomad for scheduling). Simpler intentions-based policy is sufficient.

Rare, but possible: use Consul for multi-DC service discovery and health checking across all runtimes, and Istio for fine-grained Kubernetes-only L7 mesh policy. Complexity is high; usually one or the other is sufficient.

You have fewer than ~10 services, no strict east-west security requirement, and your cloud provider's native load balancer and IAM are sufficient. Meshes add operational overhead — don't adopt one without a clear problem to solve.

Both Istio and Consul are moving toward the Kubernetes Gateway API (io.k8s.gateway.networking) as the standard ingress/mesh API, replacing their proprietary CRDs for L7 routing. Prefer Gateway API resources in new deployments for portability.
Service meshes help with service-to-service networking but do not remove broader distributed-systems or operational complexity.

A mesh does not make multi-cloud easy. Different clouds still bring separate networking, DNS, identity, load balancers, firewall rules, and failure modes. The mesh helps with east-west mTLS but not with cloud-level IAM or network topologies.
It does not fix idempotency, data consistency, saga design, poor retry semantics, or N+1 database queries. Retries at the mesh level can amplify bugs if applications are not idempotent.

You still need platform expertise, CRD lifecycle management, policy governance, observability tuning, certificate CA operations, and careful rollout/upgrade governance. A mesh adds a new control plane that must be operated.
Not a Replacement for Network Segmentation

mTLS and AuthorizationPolicy protect service-to-service traffic, but they do not replace Kubernetes NetworkPolicy, cloud security groups, or host-level firewall rules. Defense-in-depth means using all layers.

A service mesh focuses on east-west (service-to-service) traffic. It is not a full API gateway for north-south (external-to-internal) traffic management, developer portal, or API monetization. Use a dedicated API gateway (Kong, NGINX, Apigee) for that layer.

items.title: Observability, OpenTelemetry & GenAI
items.description: A practical map of observability signals, OpenTelemetry and OTLP, traces and spans, context propagation, GenAI telemetry, operating practices, and popular tools.
searchTerms: Observability is the ability to understand a system's internal state from its outputs. Telemetry is the evidence; observability is the engineering capability that turns that evidence into answers, decisions, and safer operations.
Start with questions and decisions, not dashboards. Useful telemetry helps explain user impact, locate failure domains, test hypotheses, and verify whether a change improved the system.

Telemetry is emitted data such as traces, metrics, logs, and profiles. Monitoring checks known conditions. Observability supports investigation of both known and novel failure modes by preserving useful context and relationships.

Work backward from operational questions: Which users are affected? Where is time spent? What changed? Which dependency failed? Then choose signals, attributes, retention, and views that can answer them.

Latency, traffic, errors, and saturation provide a compact service-health baseline. Add domain-specific indicators such as checkout success, queue age, model quality, or token cost when they reflect real outcomes.
Measure distributions and percentiles, not averages alone. Separate successful from failed work and, for streaming AI, distinguish time to first output from total duration.
Track demand and unsuccessful outcomes using definitions users care about. Technical 2xx responses can still be product failures, and retries can hide dependency failures while multiplying load.
Watch constrained resources and queues: CPU throttling, memory pressure, connection pools, worker utilization, queue depth, rate limits, or model concurrency.

A healthy loop detects user impact, pivots across correlated signals, forms a causal explanation, takes action, and verifies recovery. Telemetry that never changes a decision is a candidate for removal.

Signals are complementary views of the same system. Correlation through consistent resources, timestamps, trace identifiers, and domain attributes is usually more valuable than optimizing one signal in isolation.
A trace represents the path of a request or transaction across components. It is composed of spans that share a trace ID and are related through parent-child edges or explicit links.
A trace is the end-to-end execution graph. It shows critical path, fan-out, retries, queues, remote calls, and failure propagation; incomplete context propagation produces disconnected fragments.

A span records one operation with a name, start and end time, kind, attributes, events, links, status, parent relationship, resource, and instrumentation scope. Its SpanContext carries trace ID, span ID, trace flags, and trace state.

Parent-child relationships model nested causal work. Span links represent causal relationships that do not fit one parent, such as batch consumers or asynchronous fan-in. Events mark timestamped facts within a span.

Span kinds describe roles such as SERVER, CLIENT, PRODUCER, CONSUMER, and INTERNAL. Record exceptions and set status according to the semantic convention; avoid marking every non-ideal business result as a technical error.
Metrics are aggregatable measurements suited to trends, alerting, capacity, and SLOs. Their low storage cost depends on controlling attribute cardinality.
Counters represent monotonic totals, up-down counters track changing totals, gauges observe current values, and histograms preserve distributions such as latency or payload size.
Delta reports change over an interval; cumulative reports change since a start time. SDK views control aggregation and attributes, while backends must interpret temporality correctly.
Exemplars attach representative trace context to a metric data point, allowing a latency spike or histogram bucket to link directly to a concrete trace.
Logs record discrete events. Structured logs with consistent severity, resource identity, trace ID, and span ID are easier to search and correlate than unstructured text.
Prefer stable fields over parsing prose. Preserve body, timestamp, observed timestamp, severity, attributes, resource, and instrumentation scope while applying redaction before export.
Inject trace and span identifiers into log records through the logging integration. This enables a trace-to-log pivot without placing unbounded log text on every span.

Profiles explain code-level resource use such as CPU time and allocations. Correlation with traces can reveal which code paths dominate a slow request. OpenTelemetry profile support and OTLP profile transport remain under development.

OpenTelemetry is a vendor-neutral framework and specification for generating, processing, and exporting telemetry. It standardizes instrumentation and transport; it is not itself a long-term storage or visualization backend.

Application code and libraries call the API. The SDK supplies processors, samplers, readers, and exporters. Instrumentation may be manual, automatic, or provided by libraries and framework integrations.
Libraries should depend on the API so applications retain control. The application configures one SDK implementation and export path, avoiding hard-coded vendor clients in every dependency.

Language agents, hooks, or zero-code distributions instrument common frameworks quickly. Validate naming, duplicate spans, propagation, and overhead; add manual spans around business operations automation cannot infer.

A Resource identifies the entity producing telemetry, commonly with service name/version/instance and deployment environment. InstrumentationScope identifies the library or module that produced a signal.

Semantic conventions standardize span names, metric names, units, attributes, and meaning for domains such as HTTP, RPC, databases, messaging, Kubernetes, and GenAI. Pin and manage convention versions during migrations.
The Collector is a vendor-agnostic telemetry pipeline. It offloads batching, retries, filtering, enrichment, routing, sampling, and multi-backend export from application processes.

Receivers ingest or scrape data; processors batch, filter, sample, transform, or enrich it; exporters send it onward. Connectors join pipelines and extensions add operational capabilities such as health checks.

Agents run close to workloads for local collection and host context. Gateways centralize policy, routing, and tail sampling. Larger systems often combine both and scale signal-specific tiers independently.
Use memory limits, batches, sending queues, retry policies, and persistent queues where loss tolerance requires them. Backpressure and exporter saturation must be observable themselves.

Tail sampling waits for enough of a trace to choose based on errors, latency, or attributes. It preserves valuable traces but requires state, trace-aware routing, memory, and careful capacity planning.

The OpenTelemetry Protocol defines the encoding, transport, and delivery of telemetry among SDKs, Collectors, and backends. Stable OTLP support covers traces, metrics, and logs; profiles are still developing.
OTLP uses Protocol Buffers schemas grouped by Resource and InstrumentationScope. Signal-specific Export requests carry spans, metric data points, log records, or developing profile data.
OTLP/gRPC uses signal-specific gRPC Export services and binary Protobuf. Port 4317 is the default. It is efficient for long-lived service-to-collector connections.
OTLP/HTTP sends POST requests to paths such as /v1/traces, /v1/metrics, and /v1/logs on default port 4318. Payloads use binary Protobuf or Protobuf JSON, with gzip supported.

Export is request/response and can report full success, partial success, throttling, or retryable failure. Lost acknowledgements can cause retries and duplicates, so pipelines should tolerate duplicate telemetry.

Use TLS for network export, authenticate endpoints, limit receiver exposure, rotate credentials, and define egress policy. Treat telemetry as sensitive production data rather than harmless diagnostics.
Context propagation carries trace identity and optional baggage across process, network, and asynchronous boundaries so separately recorded spans can form one distributed trace.

A propagator injects context into a carrier before an outbound call and extracts it on receipt. Carriers include HTTP headers, gRPC metadata, message properties, and framework-specific request objects.

The default interoperable format uses traceparent for portable trace identity and tracestate for optional vendor-specific state. Preserve valid upstream context unless a deliberate trust-boundary policy restarts it.
The header encodes version, trace ID, parent ID, and trace flags. Each participating downstream operation creates a new span ID while keeping the trace ID, which preserves the causal chain.
An optional ordered list of vendor-specific key/value entries that accompanies a valid traceparent. It supports interoperability without putting user data into the core trace identity.

Baggage is a propagated key/value store carried beside trace context. It is not automatically a span attribute. Copy only allow-listed values into telemetry and never propagate secrets or unnecessary personal data.
Propagation must survive task scheduling, callbacks, queues, and batch processing. A consumer span may parent from one producer or link to several producer contexts when a batch has multiple causes.

Thread-local storage alone is insufficient for modern async runtimes. Use the language's supported context manager and verify propagation across executors, coroutines, reactive streams, and background jobs.
Validate inbound headers, cap baggage size, strip unsafe keys before third-party calls, and decide where public or tenant boundaries require restarting or sanitizing context.

GenAI adds nondeterministic outputs, long and streamed operations, token-based cost, retrieval, tools, agent loops, and quality evaluation. Traditional service telemetry remains necessary but is no longer sufficient.

The OpenTelemetry GenAI semantic conventions define shared spans, metrics, events, and attributes for model clients, agents, tools, retrieval, evaluations, MCP, and provider-specific behavior. They evolve independently from the core semantic-conventions repository.

Represent model operations such as chat, content generation, or text completion. Capture operation, provider, requested and response model, response ID, finish reasons, error type, duration, and token usage when available.
Model tool execution, agent invocation, embeddings, and retrieval as distinct operations so retries, handoffs, external dependencies, and the actual execution graph remain visible.

Useful measurements include client operation duration, time to first chunk, time between output chunks, input/output token usage, server request duration, time to first token, and time per output token.

Input/output messages, system instructions, tool arguments, and results can explain behavior but may contain secrets, personal data, or proprietary prompts. Treat content capture as explicit opt-in with filtering and retention controls.

Developing MCP conventions describe client/server request spans and align tool execution with GenAI spans. Record low-cardinality method and target identity; tool arguments, results, resources, and prompt variables need opt-in privacy controls.

Trace the user request through orchestration, model calls, retrieval, tools, memory, guardrails, and downstream services. Use parent-child structure for nested work and links for handoffs or other non-tree causality.

Separate query rewriting, embedding, vector search, reranking, context assembly, and generation. Capture document IDs or safe hashes, scores, counts, and latency without placing sensitive retrieved content on every span.

Track agent identity, conversation or invocation, plans, repeated model calls, tool selection, handoffs, stop conditions, retries, and loop depth. Guard against unbounded IDs becoming metric dimensions.
Total latency alone hides user experience. Measure time to first chunk or token, inter-chunk cadence, cancellation, partial output, and whether errors occurred before or after output began.

Operational health does not prove answer quality. Pair online telemetry with task-success signals and offline or sampled evaluations such as correctness, relevance, groundedness, safety, and user feedback.
Record evaluator name/version, target output, score or label, explanation where safe, dataset or experiment version, and whether evaluation is deterministic, human, heuristic, or model-based.
Attribute token usage and cost to a stable feature, workflow, model, and tenant tier where safe. Separate input, output, reasoning, and cache read/write tokens when the provider reports them.
Redact secrets and personal data, minimize prompt/response capture, protect evaluation datasets, restrict access, define short content retention, and keep auditability for model or policy changes.
Good observability is a maintained production capability. Define ownership, data contracts, reliability and cost budgets for the telemetry pipeline itself.

Begin with automatic instrumentation for broad coverage, then add manual telemetry for important business operations and failure boundaries. Standardize service naming and required resource attributes.

Align service identity, environment, version, region, tenant tier, trace IDs, deployment markers, and clocks. Use exemplars and trace/log correlation to pivot without copying high-cardinality data everywhere.

Define service-level indicators from user-visible outcomes, set objectives and error budgets, then alert on actionable burn rates or symptoms. Dashboards explain alerts; they should not be the alerting strategy.

Head sampling decides early and is efficient; tail sampling can retain errors, slow traces, or selected attributes after seeing more of the trace. Preserve complete traces and document bias introduced by sampling.
Make a consistent probability decision near trace creation, commonly from trace ID. It protects applications and pipelines but cannot know whether a downstream error will occur.
Buffer spans and decide using trace-wide evidence such as status, latency, route, or business attributes. Route all spans for a trace to the same decision point.

Never use user IDs, request IDs, raw URLs, prompts, or exception messages as metric labels. Keep high-cardinality detail in traces or logs, aggregate intentionally, and budget ingest, storage, queries, and egress.

Monitor SDK export failures and Collector accepted/refused/sent counts, queue fill, send failures, dropped data, memory, CPU, and configuration changes. A silent telemetry outage destroys confidence during incidents.
Continuously check missing service names, orphan spans, invalid durations, clock skew, schema drift, duplicate instrumentation, unexpected cardinality, and redaction failures.

Choose tools by signal coverage, query workflow, scale, retention, operational burden, cost, and standards support. OTLP and semantic conventions reduce coupling, but backend features and query languages still differ.
OpenTelemetry SDKs and Collector are the common vendor-neutral path. Prometheus scraping and remote write remain central for metrics; Fluent Bit and Vector are common log and event pipelines.
Prometheus provides pull-based metric collection, PromQL, and time-series storage; Alertmanager groups and routes alerts. Common long-term scale-out options include Grafana Mimir, Thanos, and Cortex.
Jaeger is a widely used distributed tracing system. Tempo provides object-storage-oriented trace storage and integrates closely with Grafana, logs, metrics, and exemplars.
Loki emphasizes label-based log indexing in the Grafana ecosystem. Elastic Stack and OpenSearch combine full-text search, analytics, dashboards, and log-oriented workflows.
Common managed platforms include Datadog, Dynatrace, New Relic, Splunk Observability, Honeycomb, and Grafana Cloud. OTel-native or open-source unified options include SigNoz and OpenObserve.

Common GenAI-focused options include Langfuse, Arize Phoenix, LangSmith, and Weights & Biases Weave. Compare their OpenTelemetry support, trace model, evaluation workflow, prompt/content controls, and export portability.
Grafana provides multi-source dashboards, exploration, and correlations across metrics, logs, traces, and profiles. Kibana is the primary exploration and visualization UI for Elastic data.

Roll out observability as a thin vertical slice, validate data end to end, and expand only after teams can use it. Reliability, privacy, and cost controls should arrive with instrumentation, not after an incident.

Choose one user-critical request. Instrument its entry point, dependencies, errors, golden metrics, and logs; propagate context; export through one Collector; build one useful investigation path and SLO.
Check inject/extract configuration, async context managers, message metadata, proxy header forwarding, conflicting propagators, sampling flags, and services that start new roots unexpectedly.
Trace the pipeline hop by hop: SDK creation and flush, endpoint/protocol, DNS/TLS/auth, Collector receiver, processor drops, queues, exporter errors, backend ingestion, and query time range.

Benchmark CPU, allocations, payload size, queue behavior, and shutdown flush. Batch exports, cap attributes and events, avoid synchronous network work on request paths, and define acceptable loss behavior.

Avoid dashboard-first projects, one span per tiny function, duplicate auto/manual instrumentation, sensitive payload capture by default, unbounded metric labels, alerts without owners, and collectors nobody monitors.

Assign platform and service ownership, publish naming rules, test required attributes, manage semantic-convention upgrades, review sensitive fields, and version shared dashboards and alert definitions.

items.title: Web Application Security: Browser Standards & Defenses
items.description: A practical, defense-in-depth map of web-platform security standards, browser policies, cookie sessions, authentication, authorization, input handling, APIs, and secure operations.
searchTerms: Use defense in depth: establish an encrypted origin, let browsers enforce restrictive policies, keep credentials out of untrusted code, authorize every request and object, safely handle untrusted data, and operate with least privilege. No one header or control makes an application secure.
A secure application starts with clear trust boundaries: origins, hosts, services, users, tenants, devices, and third parties. Prefer secure defaults and deny by default when a boundary is uncertain.
Serve every page and API over HTTPS with valid, current TLS configuration. Redirect HTTP to HTTPS before issuing cookies or credentials, and do not load active or passive mixed content.

Strict-Transport-Security tells a browser to use HTTPS for future requests to the host. Enable it only after HTTPS is complete; includeSubDomains and preload have wider, potentially hard-to-reverse scope.
Block HTTP scripts, styles, frames, fonts, images, and network calls from HTTPS pages. Content-Security-Policy upgrade-insecure-requests can help during migration, but fixing URLs is clearer.

Browsers isolate documents by scheme, host, and port. This baseline prevents one origin from freely reading another origin's data, but does not prevent a malicious site from sending many kinds of cross-site request.

Keep production, preview, admin, customer, and untrusted user content on deliberately chosen origins. A subdomain is not an isolation boundary for broadly scoped cookies, shared parent-domain settings, or flawed postMessage handling.
Serve user-controlled HTML and files from a separate origin without ambient application cookies. Sandboxed iframes are an additional containment layer, not a replacement for origin isolation.
For postMessage, send to an exact targetOrigin and verify event.origin and message shape before acting. Never trust a claimed origin, window name, or message payload without validation.
Response headers can make browsers enforce a smaller execution, embedding, data-sharing, and feature-use surface. Use report-only modes first where a policy could break an established application.

CSP limits the origins and types of content a page may load or execute. Build a tight per-page policy with default-src as a fallback, explicit script-src and object-src 'none', and no broad wildcards or unsafe-inline when avoidable.

Use an unpredictable per-response nonce or stable hashes for necessary inline scripts; never reuse a nonce. Trusted Types can require DOM XSS-sensitive sinks to receive reviewed TrustedHTML-like values, complementing sanitization.
Use frame-ancestors to specify exactly which sites may embed the page. It supersedes X-Frame-Options where supported and is the principal defense against clickjacking.

Deploy Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only first for complex pages, collect violation reports without sensitive payloads, then enforce. Treat reports as telemetry; do not use them as an authorization signal.

CORS is a browser read-permission protocol layered on the same-origin policy. It does not authenticate a caller, authorize an API, or stop non-browser clients. Return the smallest exact allowlist of trusted origins, methods, and headers.
When credentials are allowed, set Access-Control-Allow-Credentials only for a validated, explicit Origin and return Vary: Origin. Never combine credentialed CORS with Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *.

Browsers preflight some cross-origin requests using OPTIONS. Validate the requested origin, method, and headers at the server; cache results cautiously because permissive cached decisions broaden exposure.

Control who embeds your pages, which cross-origin resources they use, and which documents can share a browsing context group. These headers reduce clickjacking, data leaks, and cross-origin side-channel exposure.

Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy separates top-level browsing contexts; Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy requires safe opt-in for cross-origin embeds; Cross-Origin-Resource-Policy lets a resource restrict which origins may load it. Test carefully because third-party assets often need changes.
Disable browser features such as camera, microphone, geolocation, payment, or fullscreen unless a page needs them. Delegate a capability to an iframe only through an intentional allowlist.
Use strict-origin-when-cross-origin or a stricter policy to avoid disclosing full paths and query strings to other origins. Never place secrets or bearer tokens in URLs, regardless of this header.

For static third-party scripts or styles, integrity hashes let the browser reject bytes that do not match the expected asset. Pin versions, review the supply chain, and pair SRI with a restrictive CSP; a CDN compromise can still affect resources you repin.

Authentication establishes a principal; a session maintains that result; authorization decides an action. Keep browser-exposed credential material minimal, short-lived, purpose-bound, and revocable where risk warrants it.

A Secure, HttpOnly cookie containing an opaque session identifier protects that identifier from JavaScript and is usually preferable to exposing an OAuth access token to browser code. Scope the cookie narrowly and keep access and refresh tokens on a backend-for-frontend when possible.

Set Secure and HttpOnly. Choose SameSite=Lax or Strict when the product allows it; use SameSite=None only for necessary cross-site use and always with Secure. Omit Domain to make a host-only cookie, and use the smallest practical Path, while remembering Path is not an access-control boundary.

Prefer __Host- for primary host cookies: it requires Secure, Path=/, and no Domain, preventing subdomain scoping. __Secure- requires Secure. Partitioned cookies can limit third-party cookie state per top-level site but do not replace session design.

Generate session IDs with a cryptographically secure random source, rotate them after login or privilege changes, expire idle and absolute sessions, invalidate on logout and compromise, and limit concurrent sessions according to risk.

Because cookies may be attached automatically, protect every state-changing cookie-authenticated endpoint with SameSite plus a server-validated anti-CSRF token or an equivalent origin-bound design. Verify Origin or Referer as defense in depth, and never use GET to change state.

Use authorization code flow with PKCE for browser sign-in. Validate redirect URIs, state, nonce, issuer, audience, signature, expiry, and authorization context. An ID token identifies an authentication event; it is not an API access token.
Avoid localStorage and sessionStorage for long-lived bearer credentials because XSS can read them. A BFF can keep OAuth tokens server-side and expose only an HttpOnly session cookie to the browser.

Prefer phishing-resistant WebAuthn passkeys or security keys for sensitive accounts. Require fresh or stronger authentication for high-risk actions and ensure recovery paths do not silently downgrade assurance.

If passwords are supported, hash them with a modern adaptive password hash such as Argon2id, rate-limit and monitor login attempts, allow password managers, avoid security questions, and make reset tokens single-use, short-lived, and high entropy.

Treat every request, parameter, file, callback, and queued message as untrusted. Enforce authorization at the server on every access, not in UI logic, token appearance, client-supplied claims, or network location.

Deny by default and make a server-side decision for every action. Combine tenant, principal, role, ownership, relationship, resource state, and business policy as applicable; cache carefully and re-evaluate after privilege changes.

Prevent IDOR/BOLA by loading or checking each requested object in the authenticated principal's authorized tenant and scope. Never trust an object ID, user ID, role, or tenant ID supplied by the client.

Use distinct roles and service identities, narrow OAuth scopes and audiences, time-bound elevated access, and separate admin interfaces. Log authorization decisions for sensitive actions without logging secrets.

Use framework auto-escaping and contextual output encoding for HTML, attributes, URLs, JavaScript, and CSS. Avoid dangerous DOM sinks such as innerHTML; when HTML is required, sanitize with a maintained allowlist and preserve CSP as a backstop.

Validate type, length, format, range, structure, and business rules at every trust boundary. Use parameterized queries and safe APIs for SQL, NoSQL, LDAP, commands, templates, and URLs; validation complements rather than replaces parameterization.

For server-side URL fetching, use an allowlist of schemes, destinations, ports, redirects, and response sizes. Resolve and recheck destinations to prevent access to loopback, link-local, internal, or cloud metadata services.

Authenticate and authorize uploads, validate content independently of filename and MIME claim, enforce size limits, scan as appropriate, generate server-side names, and store outside the executable web root or on a separate file origin.
Avoid native object deserialization of untrusted bytes. Apply schemas and resource limits to JSON, XML, archives, images, and document parsers; disable XML external entities unless explicitly needed.

Set request size, rate, concurrency, pagination, query-complexity, and timeout limits. Authenticate before expensive work where possible, use idempotency keys for retriable writes, and return errors that are useful without revealing internals.

Sec-Fetch-Site, Sec-Fetch-Mode, and related request headers can help reject unexpected cross-site browser requests. Use them as a supplemental policy because they are browser signals, not universal client authentication.

Verify a signature over the raw body using a per-sender secret or public key, enforce timestamp and replay protection, allowlist callback URLs, and make processing idempotent. Do not trust source IP alone.

Security continues after code ships: protect secrets and build systems, understand third parties, observe high-value events, patch quickly, and rehearse recovery. Production configuration is code worthy of review and testing.

Keep secrets out of source, browser bundles, URLs, logs, and error reports. Use a managed secret store, scoped workload identity, encryption in transit and at rest, rotation, access audit trails, and rapid revocation paths.

Pin and review dependencies, lock package resolution, remove unused packages, scan for known vulnerabilities, protect CI permissions, verify release provenance where available, and assess every third-party script or service as a trust decision.

Set CSP, HSTS, Referrer-Policy, Permissions-Policy, and an appropriate frame-ancestors policy deliberately. X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff prevents certain MIME-sniffing risks. Do not rely on legacy X-XSS-Protection as an XSS defense.

Log authentication, authorization failures, privilege changes, administrative actions, webhook verification failures, and suspicious rate-limit events with correlation IDs. Redact secrets, tokens, passwords, and unnecessary personal data; alert, investigate, contain, and learn through rehearsed incident response.

Use threat modeling, code review, dependency and secret scanning, tests for authorization boundaries, dynamic testing, configuration review, and periodic penetration testing. Retest after architecture, authentication, or data-flow changes.

Prioritize controls by the data, privileges, exposure, exploitability, and blast radius in your application. Link each threat to prevention, detection, and recovery rather than relying on a generic checklist.

An attacker gets script to run in a trusted origin, enabling UI manipulation and access to data that page scripts can access. Prevent with safe rendering and sanitization; CSP limits impact; HttpOnly cookies reduce but do not eliminate session abuse.
A hostile site frames a trusted page and tricks a user into clicking it. Use CSP frame-ancestors, explicit embed allowlists, and confirmation or reauthentication for high-impact actions.

Phishing, malware, exposed tokens, session fixation, insecure recovery, and over-broad cookie scope can lead to account takeover. Use passkeys or MFA, secure session lifecycle, scoped cookies, anomaly detection, and fast revocation.

Over-broad APIs, missing object checks, permissive CORS, sensitive URLs, verbose errors, logs, caches, and third-party scripts can disclose data. Minimize collection and disclosure, encrypt appropriately, and enforce authorization on each object.
